lead: Hierarchical clustering builds a tree of clusters instead of one fixed partition. It matters when you do not know k, the number of clusters, in advance or want to see how groups form at different distance scales. Agglomerative clustering starts with every point alone and merges the closest pair again and again; divisive clustering starts with all points together and splits. The tree, called a dendrogram, records the height of every merge or split. It is used in customer segmentation, gene expression analysis, document grouping and fault diagnosis on a network.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for clusters and distances, and the distance review in Unit 1.

sections.h3: Agglomerative clustering: merge from the bottom

blocks.text: Agglomerative clustering is bottom-up. Start with n points. Put each point in its own singleton cluster, so there are n clusters. Define a linkage rule that gives a distance between any two clusters. At every step, find the pair of clusters with the smallest linkage distance. Merge that pair and record the distance as the merge height. Repeat until one cluster remains. This takes n − 1 merges.

items: Start: n singleton clusters, one per point.
Compute the linkage distance for every cluster pair.
Merge the pair with the smallest distance.
Record that distance as the height of the new join.
Stop when one cluster remains, or earlier if a cut is chosen.

blocks.text: d<sub>single</sub>(A,B) = min d(a,b) for a in A, b in B
blocks.where: A and B are clusters; a and b are points; d(a,b) is the point distance, such as Euclidean distance.

blocks.text: The first merge joins the two closest points. Every later merge joins two groups, not just two points. The order of merges and their heights form the cluster tree, drawn as a dendrogram.
The linkage rule decides what closest means between two clusters. A different rule can give a different tree from the same data. Four rules are common.

items: Single linkage: use the smallest distance between any point in A and any point in B. It can chain long clusters.
Complete linkage: use the largest distance between any point in A and any point in B. It prefers compact clusters.
Average linkage: use the average of all cross distances between points in A and points in B.
Ward linkage: merge the pair that gives the smallest increase in the total within-cluster sum of squares.

blocks.where: ΔSSE is the increase in within-cluster sum of squares if A and B merge; |A| and |B| are cluster sizes; μ<sub>A</sub> and μ<sub>B</sub> are cluster means; ||x|| is Euclidean length.

blocks.text: Ward works with squared Euclidean distance and tends to make equal-sized, compact clusters. Single linkage can follow a chain of points. Complete and average sit between these extremes.

sections.h3: Divisive clustering and reading a dendrogram

blocks.text: Divisive clustering is top-down. Start with all n points in one cluster. At each step, choose one cluster and split it into two. A common split runs a flat method such as k-means inside that cluster, or removes the longest links in a minimum spanning tree. Stop when every point is alone, or when a stopping rule is met. Divisive clustering needs a rule for which cluster to split and how to split it.

A dendrogram is the picture of the merge or split history. Leaves are the original points. A join is a merge; its height is the distance at which the merge happened. For the five points 1, 2, 4, 8, 9 under single linkage, p1 and p2 join at height 1, p8 and p9 also join at height 1, p4 joins {1,2} at height 2, and the two groups {1,2,4} and {8,9} join at height 4.

To get clusters, cut the dendrogram with a horizontal line at height h. Each vertical line crossed by the cut is one cluster. The cut height is a distance, not a cluster count. Choose h from the problem, or compare cuts with cluster evaluation in Chapter 4.8. Some syllabi call this hierarchical cluster analysis.

figure.caption: A dendrogram for five points. p1 and p2 join at height 1, p8 and p9 join at height 1, p4 joins at height 2, and the two groups join at height 4; a cut between heights 2 and 4 gives two clusters.

spec.aria: A dendrogram for five points p1,p2,p4,p8,p9 merges p1 with p2 at height 1, merges p8 with p9 at height 1, joins p4 at height 2, and joins the two groups at height 4.

examples.question: Five points on a line have values 1, 2, 4, 8 and 9. Use single-link agglomerative clustering. List the merge heights in order and give the two clusters from cutting the dendrogram between the two highest merge levels.
steps: List the smallest point distances: d(1,2)=1 and d(8,9)=1. The other near distances are d(2,4)=2 and d(4,8)=4.
Merge {1} and {2} at height 1. Merge {8} and {9} at height 1. Clusters now: {1,2}, {4}, {8,9}.
The smallest is 2, so merge {1,2} with {4} at height 2. Clusters now: {1,2,4}, {8,9}.
Distance between {1,2,4} and {8,9} is min(4,5,6,7,7,8) = 4. Merge at height 4.
Merge heights in order: 1, 1, 2, 4. A cut between heights 2 and 4, for example h=3, crosses two vertical lines.
examples.answer: The merge heights are 1, 1, 2, 4 in the same units as the point values; the cut gives clusters {1, 2, 4} and {8, 9}.

traps: A cut height is a distance, not a cluster count. At h=3 the five-point example gives two clusters, but at h=1.5 it gives three.
Linkage choice changes the dendrogram. Single, complete, average and Ward can give different merges on the same data.
Single linkage can chain: one close bridge can join two large groups that are far apart.
Ties are common. Two pairs at height 1 can be merged in either order; the set of heights stays the same, but the drawn tree may look different.
Changing units or scaling features changes distances and may change the hierarchy. Standardise features when units differ.

quiz.q: What does a leaf of a dendrogram represent?
quiz.a: One original data point, or a singleton cluster at the start.

quiz.q: Why does a horizontal cut of a dendrogram give clusters?
quiz.a: Merges above the cut have not happened at that distance, so each vertical line crossing the cut is a separate group.

quiz.q: For points 0, 2, 5, 9, find the single-link and complete-link distances between clusters {0,2} and {5,9}.
quiz.a: Cross distances are 5, 9, 3, 7. Single-link = min = 3. Complete-link = max = 9.

quiz.q: Two dendrograms from the same data use single and complete linkage. Which is more likely to chain, and why?
quiz.a: Single linkage, because it uses the minimum cross distance; one close pair can merge two groups that are otherwise far apart.
Top-down hierarchical clustering: start with one cluster and split clusters until a stopping rule.

quiz.q: What does Ward linkage minimise when two clusters merge?
quiz.a: The increase in within-cluster sum of squares, ΔSSE.

quiz.q: A dendrogram has merge heights 1, 1, 2, 4. How many clusters does a cut at h=1.5 give? At h=3?
quiz.a: At h=1.5, the two height-1 merges have happened, so three clusters: {1,2}, {4}, {8,9}. At h=3, the height-2 merge has also happened, so two clusters: {1,2,4} and {8,9}.

beyond: Not for the exam. Hierarchical clustering is used in single-cell RNA analysis, customer segmentation, document grouping and network fault diagnosis. Scalable versions use nearest-neighbour chains and constrained clustering for large data. Search for hierarchical clustering linkage, Ward method, dendrogram cut, and HDBSCAN.
